lessons.title: Price-to-Book and Dividend Yield: Asset-Heavy and Income Stocks

children.text: P/E and EV/EBITDA value a company on what it earns. Two other multiples start from different places. Price-to-book compares the share price with the accounting value of what shareholders own. Dividend yield compares it with the cash shareholders actually receive. Both are indispensable for certain Indian stocks, especially banks, NBFCs and high-dividend PSUs, and both are easy to misread when looked at alone.

body.text: Price-to-book means nothing without return on equity: a bank earning less than its cost of equity deserves to trade below book. Dividend yield means nothing without sustainability: a high yield from a shrinking, over-distributing business is a warning, not income.

children.text: Price-to-Book: What It Measures

body.latex: \text{P/B} = \frac{\text{Share price}}{\text{Book value per share}} = \frac{\text{Market capitalisation}}{\text{Shareholders' equity (net worth)}}
body.caption: Book value = total assets minus total liabilities, as reported on the balance sheet

children.text: Book value
is an accounting number. How close it sits to economic reality depends entirely on the kind of business.

markDefs.definition: Shareholders' equity as recorded on the balance sheet: share capital plus reserves and surplus. It reflects historical cost accounting, not market value.

columns.label: Book value is a good anchor
points: Banks, NBFCs and insurers: assets are mostly loans and investments carried near realistic values
Asset-heavy cyclicals near a trough, where book gives a rough floor
Capital-intensive businesses whose assets are recent and not heavily depreciated

columns.label: Book value tells you little
points: Brand-led FMCG and consumer companies: brands built through advertising are not on the balance sheet
IT services and software: the key assets are people and client relationships
Companies with large buybacks, which shrink book value
Companies with accumulated losses, where book can be tiny or negative

children.text: This is why Indian consumer companies with powerful brands often trade at 10 or more times book value while still being reasonable investments, and why a bank at 3 times book can be far more expensive than it looks.
The P/B-ROE Link
Chapter 1 showed that a P/E is a compressed DCF. The same is true of P/B. For a company that grows at g forever, with return on equity ROE and cost of equity Ke, the price-to-book it deserves is:

body.caption: Assumes a steady ROE, growth below the cost of equity and payout consistent with that growth

body.label: The single most useful rule for valuing lenders
body.context: A bank earning exactly its cost of equity is worth exactly its book value. Earn more, and each rupee of book is worth more than a rupee. Earn less, and it is worth less, no matter how cheap the P/B looks.

body.caption: Justified P/B at a 12.0% cost of equity and 6.0% perpetual growth

children.text: Worked Example: Three Lenders
Three fictional listed Indian lenders, each with a cost of equity reflecting its risk and a sustainable long-term growth rate.

Godavari Bank trades below book at 0.8×, and a screen for "banks below book value" would flag it as cheap. But with an ROE of 9.0% against a 14.0% cost of equity, it destroys value on every rupee it retains. Its justified P/B is only 0.38×, so at 0.8× it is the most expensive of the three relative to its fundamentals. During the bad loan cycle of the late 2010s, many Indian public sector banks traded well below book value for exactly this reason: low or negative ROE, not market irrationality.

body.text: The formula is very sensitive to the gap between ROE and growth, and between cost of equity and growth. Small changes in assumed long-term ROE move the justified P/B a lot. Use it to understand what a P/B implies about sustainable ROE, not as a precise target. For Shivalik Finance, a P/B of 3.8× implies the market expects its ROE to stay well above 21.0% for a long time, or its risk to fall.

children.text: Adjusting book value for bad loans
A bank's book value assumes its loans will be repaid. When they will not, book value is overstated. Indian analysts often use
price to adjusted book value (P/ABV)
, which deducts an estimate of further losses on net non-performing assets.

markDefs.definition: Share price divided by book value per share after deducting an estimate of further losses on bad loans, typically a share of net non-performing assets, net of tax.

Dividend Yield: What It Measures

body.latex: \text{Dividend yield} = \frac{\text{Dividend per share over the last 12 months}}{\text{Share price}}
body.caption: Include interim and final dividends; exclude one-off special dividends when judging sustainable yield

children.text: Rearrange the dividend discount model, price = next year's dividend ÷ (Ke - g), and a simple, powerful relationship appears: expected return ≈ dividend yield + long-term dividend growth. A low yield is not a problem if growth is high, and a high yield is not a bargain if growth is negative.

body.caption: Yield plus growth: three illustrative income profiles

children.text: The PSU energy company pays the most today; the private bank pays the least. Yet in this illustration the private bank's expected return is the highest, because it reinvests profit at a high ROE to grow, while the PSU returns cash now and grows slowly. A higher yield is not the same as a higher return. Several PSU stocks, such as Coal India and ONGC, have long been known for high dividend yields, while many high-ROE private sector companies pay out little and grow instead.

body.caption: Sustainable growth from retained earnings, assuming ROE is stable

children.text: A company with a 20.0% ROE that pays out 40.0% of profit can grow at about 12.0% a year from retained earnings alone. Pay out more, and growth slows. Pay out more than 100% for long, and the business shrinks or borrows.
After-Tax Yield: What Indian Investors Actually Keep

Dividends in India are taxed in the hands of shareholders at their income tax slab rate. That changes the comparison between high-dividend stocks and growth stocks, whose gains are taxed as capital gains only when shares are sold.

body.title: How dividend and buyback taxation has changed for shareholders

events.title: Dividend distribution tax abolished
events.description: Companies no longer pay DDT. Dividends become taxable in shareholders' hands at their slab rates, with TDS deducted above a threshold.

events.title: Capital gains rates revised
events.description: Long-term capital gains on listed equity become taxable at 12.5% above an annual exemption of ₹1.25 lakh; short-term gains at 20%.

events.title: Buybacks taxed as dividends
events.description: Amounts received in share buybacks are taxed as dividend income in shareholders' hands, with the cost of the shares treated as a capital loss.

body.text: For an investor in the 30% slab, a 6% dividend yield becomes about 4.1% after tax, similar to the post-tax return on many bank fixed deposits, but with equity risk. Always compare dividend yields with alternatives on an after-tax basis, and remember that long-term capital gains on equity are taxed at a lower rate than slab-rate dividends for most high-income investors.

children.text: The Dividend Yield Trap

Coastal Power & Mining Ltd is a fictional NSE-listed company. A year ago its shares traded at ₹250 and it paid a dividend of ₹12 per share, a 4.8% yield. Since then, a regulatory change has cut its tariffs. EPS has fallen from ₹20 to ₹8, free cash flow has turned negative, and the share price has fallen 60% to ₹100. The board has kept the dividend at ₹12, and a stock screener now shows a 12.0% dividend yield.

stats.label: Share price change
stats.context: The yield rose because the price fell

children.text: The 12.0% yield is not a sign of value. It is the arithmetic result of a collapsing share price and a dividend the company can no longer afford. Paying 150% of earnings with negative free cash flow means the dividend is being funded with debt. Unless earnings recover quickly, it will be cut, and the yield will vanish.

body.title: Is this dividend safe? Check on screener.in
steps: Payout ratio: is the dividend below net profit, ideally with room to spare, over the last five years?
Free cash flow: has cash from operations minus capex covered the dividend in most years?
Trend: are profits and cash flows stable or growing, or falling?
Debt: is borrowing rising while dividends are maintained?
Price: has a high yield appeared mainly because the share price has fallen sharply?
Special dividends: is the trailing yield inflated by a one-off payment?
Ownership: for PSUs, is the dividend driven by the government's need for revenue rather than the company's surplus cash?

body.caption: When to lead with P/B or dividend yield

cells: ROE, cost of equity, asset quality
P/B on market value of stakes
Payout ratio, FCF coverage, after-tax yield

children.text: Check Your Understanding

body.title: Justified P/B
body.prompt: A private sector bank has a sustainable ROE of 18%, a cost of equity of 13% and long-term growth of 7%. What is its justified P/B? Answer to two decimal places.

body.title: After-tax dividend yield
body.prompt: An investor in the 30% tax slab, paying 4% health and education cess and no surcharge, buys a stock with a 6% dividend yield. What is the post-tax yield, in %? Answer to two decimal places.

body.title: The bank below book
body.question: A listed bank trades at 0.7× book value. Its sustainable ROE is 8%, its cost of equity is 13% and long-term growth is 6%. What does the P/B-ROE framework suggest?
options: It is cheap because it trades below book value
It may be expensive: its justified P/B is only about 0.29×, because ROE is well below its cost of equity
It is fairly valued because all banks should trade near book
P/B cannot be used for banks
body.explanation: Justified P/B = (8% - 6%) ÷ (13% - 6%) = 0.29×. A bank earning less than its cost of equity destroys value on retained capital, so trading below book is not automatically cheap. The key question is whether ROE will improve.

body.title: The break-even point
body.textWithBlank: When a company's sustainable ROE equals its cost of equity, its justified P/B equals ___.
body.explanation: (ROE - g) ÷ (Ke - g) = 1 when ROE = Ke. The company is worth exactly its book value.

body.title: The retired father's income portfolio
body.scenario: Sunita, a Coimbatore-based software engineer, is helping her retired father, who is in the 30% tax slab, build a monthly income portfolio. A relative recommends putting ₹20 lakh into three stocks with dividend yields of 9%, 11% and 14%, saying "much better than an FD". Sunita checks screener.in: all three share prices have fallen 40% to 60% in the past year; two have payout ratios above 100%; one has negative free cash flow for three years and rising debt; and one paid a large special dividend last year that is included in the trailing yield.
body.prompt: What should Sunita tell her father about these "high-yield" stocks, and what should she look for instead?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The high yields are mostly the result of falling prices. A 40% to 60% fall usually reflects a real deterioration in the business, not an opportunity.
2. Payouts above 100% are not sustainable. A company paying more than it earns must use cash reserves or borrowing, and will usually cut the dividend.
3. Negative free cash flow and rising debt confirm the dividend is being funded with borrowed money.
4. The special dividend inflates the trailing yield. The ongoing yield is much lower.
5. After tax at 31.2%, even a genuine 9% yield is about 6.2%, and a cut dividend could leave far less, with the capital itself at risk.
6. Compared with an FD, these stocks add equity risk and concentration risk to money her father may need for regular expenses.

What to look for instead: companies with moderate yields, payout ratios comfortably below 100%, free cash flow that covers dividends in most years, stable or growing profits and low debt; spread across several companies and sectors. She should also consider whether part of the income need is better met through debt instruments, and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser for a retirement income plan.

points: P/B compares price with accounting book value. It is meaningful for banks, NBFCs, insurers and asset-heavy businesses, and weak for brand-led and asset-light companies.
Justified P/B = (ROE - g) ÷ (Ke - g). A company earning its cost of equity is worth book value; below it, less than book.
A bank below book value can still be expensive if its ROE is below its cost of equity.
Expected return ≈ dividend yield + long-term dividend growth. High yield and high growth rarely come together.
Dividends are taxed at slab rates in India. Compare yields after tax, including with FDs and capital gains.
A high yield caused by a falling price, a payout above 100% or negative free cash flow is usually a trap.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or tax advice. Godavari Bank, Narmadapuram Private Bank, Shivalik Finance, Coastal Power & Mining Ltd and the individuals named are fictional, and their figures are illustrative. References to Coal India and ONGC are historical and are not recommendations. Tax rules and thresholds change and depend on individual circumstances; consult a chartered accountant and a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making decisions.
